content: This document does not address the off-label use of products or investigational products, except where some recommendations may differ from the product's package labeling. The CDC does not accept commercial support. Unintended pregnancy rates in the United States remain high, with approximately 50% of all pregnancies being unintended. These rates are disproportionately higher among adolescents, young women, women from racial or ethnic minority groups, and women with lower levels of education and income. Unintended pregnancies are associated with increased risks of adverse maternal and infant outcomes and, in 2002, resulted in $5 billion in direct medical costs in the United States. Approximately half of unintended pregnancies occur in women who were not using contraception at the time of conception, while the other half occur in women who became pregnant despite reported contraceptive use. Strategies to prevent unintended pregnancies include assisting women and their partners in selecting appropriate contraceptive methods and ensuring correct and consistent use of these methods. In 2010, the CDC adapted global guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO) to help healthcare providers counsel individuals and couples on contraceptive method choices. This guidance, known as the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR), focuses on the optimal use of contraceptive methods for individuals of all ages, including adolescents. Over the past 15 years, the CDC has contributed to the development and updating of WHO's global family planning guidance by critically appraising and synthesizing scientific evidence. The WHO first published the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (WHO SPR) in 2002, providing evidence-based global guidance on the safe and effective use of contraceptive methods. Since then, WHO has regularly updated this guidance based on new evidence, with the document now in its second edition, including an additional update in 2008. WHO's global guidance is intended for use by policymakers, family planning program managers, and the scientific community as a reference for developing countryor program-specific family planning guidance, rather than for direct use by healthcare providers. The CDC has adapted the WHO SPR for the United States, removing guidance on contraceptive methods not available in the U.S. and adding new topics, such as the effectiveness of female sterilization, extended use of combined hormonal methods, transitioning to regular contraception after emergency contraception, and determining when contraception is no longer needed. This document provides recommendations for healthcare providers on the safe and effective use of contraceptive methods, addressing their provision, management of side effects, and other issues related to contraceptive use. Although the term woman is used throughout the document, the recommendations apply to all females of reproductive age, including adolescents. Adolescents are identified as a special population that may benefit from more frequent follow-up. These recommendations are intended to serve as clinical guidance for healthcare providers, who should always consider the individual clinical circumstances of each person seeking family planning services. This report is not a substitute for professional medical advice for individual patients, and individuals should consult their healthcare providers when considering family planning options. The CDC initiated a process to adapt the WHO SPR for the United States, which included determining the scope of the adaptation, preparing systematic reviews of evidence, convening expert meetings, and finalizing recommendations. Specific WHO recommendations were modified based on new scientific evidence or the context of family planning services in the U.S. Additional recommendations were added, and information about methods not available in the U.S. was removed. Systematic reviews were conducted to assess evidence related to clinical challenges associated with the recommendations, and these reviews were peer-reviewed by experts. In October 2011, the CDC convened a meeting of 36 experts, including obstetrician-gynecologists, pediatricians, family physicians, nurse-midwives, nurse practitioners, and epidemiologists, to assist in guideline development and provide input on the evidence and recommendations. Feedback was also obtained from an external review panel of healthcare providers who had not participated in the adaptation meetings. Areas requiring further research were also identified. The recommendations in this document are intended to help healthcare providers address issues related to contraceptive use, such as initiating a method, necessary examinations and tests, follow-up care, and managing common problems like missed pills and side effects. Recommendations are organized by contraceptive method, generally presented in order of effectiveness, from highest to lowest. The document does not provide guidance on every aspect of contraceptive provision and management but focuses on specific issues using the best available evidence. Recommendations are provided for permanent methods like vasectomy and female sterilization, as well as reversible methods such as copper intrauterine devices (Cu-IUDs), levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs), etonogestrel implants, progestin-only injectables, progestin-only pills (POPs), combined hormonal contraceptives (including pills, patches, and vaginal rings), and the standard days method (SDM). Guidance is also provided for emergency contraception, including the Cu-IUD and emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs). For each method, recommendations address the timing of initiation, the need for additional contraception or backup methods, and the examinations and tests required before initiation. Most women require few or no tests before starting a contraceptive method. A classification system developed by WHO and adopted by the CDC categorizes the applicability of various examinations and tests before initiating contraceptive methods. The document includes systematic reviews of evidence for screening tests associated with the safe use of contraceptive methods. Summary charts and clinical algorithms have been developed to assist healthcare providers in managing family planning patients, including guidance on when to start specific methods, necessary examinations and tests, routine follow-up, and management of bleeding irregularities. The CDC will continue to work with WHO to identify and assess new evidence and update recommendations as needed. The CDC SPR will follow updates to WHO guidance, which typically occur every 3-4 years or sooner if warranted by new data. In most cases, a detailed history provides the most accurate assessment of pregnancy risk in a woman about to start using contraception. Several criteria for assessing pregnancy risk are provided, and healthcare providers are encouraged to use these criteria to determine whether a woman is not pregnant. Routine pregnancy testing is not necessary for every woman, but a urine pregnancy test may be considered based on clinical judgment. For contraceptive methods other than IUDs, the benefits of starting contraception likely outweigh any risks, even if the healthcare provider is uncertain whether the woman is pregnant. In such cases, follow-up pregnancy testing in 2-4 weeks may be considered. For women who wish to use an IUD, another contraceptive method should be provided until pregnancy can be ruled out.
